domain: Terminal session capture and remote control on macOS (tmux, node-pty, TUI rendering on phone, scrollback replay)
recommendation: Make tmux the single capture layer for both plain shells and TUI agents: a Node daemon (launchd LaunchAgent, same user) speaks tmux control mode (`tmux -C attach`) over the default per-user socket — it lists sessions, streams live output via %output, injects input via send-keys, replays scrollback on phone connect via `capture-pane -p -e -S -`, and enables pause-mode flow control (`refresh-client -f pause-after=...`) so fast build logs cannot flood the phone link. Remote-started tasks are `tmux new-session -d -c <projectdir>` from the daemon (node-pty is only needed to host the `tmux -C` client process and any non-tmux one-off jobs); user-opened terminals become controllable by setting VS Code's default terminal profile to a tmux wrapper (`tmux new -A -s vscode-N`), which also gives free crash/disconnect persistence. Terminals NOT inside tmux are best-effort only: the VS Code extension arm can read command output through the stable shell-integration API and send input via sendText, but cannot capture raw TUI streams — say so in the UI rather than pretending. On the phone, render panes with xterm.js at the pane's actual laptop-side size (80–120 cols) with horizontal pan/pinch-zoom; never resize the PTY to phone width, because Claude Code's ink UI demonstrably corrupts on resize — if the user wants a phone-native view of an agent, that should come from the Agent SDK stream-json channel, with the terminal view as the fallback 'exact screen' mirror. Skip ttyd/GoTTY/tty-share/upterm as components — they solve public sharing, not private mirroring — but copy their architecture: raw PTY bytes over one WebSocket, xterm.js client, flow control, and optionally @xterm/headless + serialize addon server-side if you want instant reconnect snapshots without asking tmux.
pitfalls: Resizing the shared PTY to phone width wrecks the laptop view: with window-size=latest (the default), any client that registers a size wins, and Claude Code's ink UI loses content and floods scrollback on every resize step. Keep the phone a control-mode client that never issues refresh-client -C.

%output payloads are octal-escaped and can split UTF-8 and ANSI escape sequences across notifications; decode to raw bytes first and feed them to xterm.js untouched, or colors and box-drawing will corrupt.

pipe-pane only captures FUTURE output and allows one pipe per pane; connect-time state must come from capture-pane. And history-limit changes only apply to windows created afterward — set it before spawning sessions.

You cannot retro-attach existing plain terminals — the tmux wrapper profile only covers terminals opened AFTER setup, and users will still have non-tmux terminals you can't see. Design the session list to show 'visible/controllable' vs 'not capturable' honestly.

VS Code shell-integration capture is command-scoped: it reads output of executed commands, not the raw stream, and shell integration injection inside tmux is historically flaky (Cline-style 'shell integration unavailable' failures) [UNVERIFIED for current VS Code versions].

Driving an AI agent by scraping its ink TUI (parsing screen text to find approval prompts) is fragile across Claude Code releases; use the Agent SDK canUseTool/stream-json for the approvals inbox and treat tmux capture purely as a live screen mirror.
Without flow control, one `yarn build` in a pane can buffer megabytes to a phone on LTE; tmux pause-mode or a ttyd-style ack/resume scheme is not optional polish, it is required.

ttyd defaults to read-only clients and one process per connection — if you evaluate it as a shortcut, state persistence still requires tmux underneath, at which point you've built the recommended architecture anyway.
GoTTY (yudai) is abandoned; anything copied from it should come from the sorenisanerd fork.

The daemon must run as the logged-in user (LaunchAgent, not LaunchDaemon) or it lands on a different tmux socket (/private/tmp/tmux-<uid>/default) and sees zero user sessions; also nothing works if the laptop sleeps — pmset/caffeinate config is a setup prerequisite.

tmux is not currently installed on the user's machine — 'brew install tmux' is a hard prerequisite, and the VS Code terminal profile change should use 'tmux new -A' so it attaches instead of erroring when a session name exists.

domain: VS Code companion extension capabilities (July 2026): terminal/shell-integration APIs, tasks and window state, cross-extension limits, Remote Tunnels escape hatch, and the extension-vs-daemon split
recommendation: The standalone daemon must be the source of truth and own everything that has to survive VS Code being closed: hosting agent sessions via the Claude Agent SDK (canUseTool approvals, includePartialMessages streaming, --resume), the approvals inbox, push notifications, phone transport, starting new tasks, and any terminal the system itself spawns — node-pty in the daemon gives full raw I/O with zero VS Code restrictions, so never run 'controlled' terminals inside VS Code. The companion extension should be a thin sensor/actuator that connects outward to the daemon over localhost WebSocket and contributes only what requires being inside the IDE: mirroring user-opened integrated terminals (subscribe to onDidStartTerminalShellExecution, call execution.read() immediately, pipe raw ANSI to the daemon), injecting input via Terminal.sendText, and reporting IDE state (workspace folders, active editor, tabs, window focus, terminal list with shell type and cwd). Treat integrated-terminal mirroring as best-effort observation, not control: attach-at-start-only semantics mean a Claude Code TUI launched before the extension activated is invisible, so the product should steer users to launch agents through the daemon. Do not attempt to read or drive the Claude Code chat panel — webview isolation makes it impossible; at most invoke its registered commands to focus/open it. Keep 'code tunnel' + vscode.dev (or 'code serve-web' over Tailscale) as a documented full-IDE escape hatch from the phone browser, not as a product component.
pitfalls: read() attach-at-start-only: output before the first read() call is lost forever, and there is no stable API to read an existing terminal buffer — a long-running TUI (claude, vim, htop) started before the extension subscribed can never be mirrored; restarting VS Code or reloading the extension drops all live streams

Raw execution output is ANSI/VT data including alt-screen sequences; Claude Code's TUI output appended as plain text is garbage — the daemon needs a headless terminal emulator (e.g. @xterm/headless) per mirrored session to reconstruct screen state for the phone

Shell integration silently fails to activate on nonstandard zsh configs (powerlevel10k instant prompt, custom PROMPT_COMMAND hooks are known offenders); design the extension to degrade to 'terminal exists, input-only, no output' rather than assuming read() is available
Do not build on onDidWriteTerminalData: it is a forever-proposed API, blocked for Marketplace extensions, and Microsoft has said it will not be stabilized
One extension host per VS Code window: the extension only sees its own window's terminals; with multiple windows the daemon receives multiple extension connections and must namespace/aggregate them

sendText with shouldExecute default true appends Enter — for TUI steering send shouldExecute=false and explicit sequences ('\r', '\x1b[A', '\x03' for Ctrl-C); also sendText into the wrong terminal is remote command execution, so the daemon must verify terminal identity before routing phone input
Tasks API gives start/end/exit-code only — do not promise task output streaming on the phone from the Tasks API; run anything needing output capture through the daemon's own pty instead

The Claude Code chat panel is a dead end (webview isolation); its command IDs are undocumented and can change without notice — anything beyond 'focus the panel' will break silently on extension updates

Tunnel escape hatch caveats: requires GitHub OAuth in the phone browser, 10-tunnel account cap, tunnel process must stay running, and the mobile UX for agent permission dialogs is bad enough that it cannot substitute for the phone app's approvals inbox

code serve-web bound to 0.0.0.0 or with --without-connection-token is an unauthenticated remote IDE with terminal access — if used at all, bind to the Tailscale interface only and keep the connection token

domain: Programmatically driving AI coding agents (Claude Agent SDK, ACP, Codex, OpenCode, PTY fallback) — July 2026
recommendation: Build the hub as a Node/TypeScript daemon with a small internal session/approval event model and three adapter tiers — do NOT go ACP-only. Tier 1 (Claude, native): drive Claude via @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk directly — canUseTool for the approvals inbox (including AskUserQuestion multiple-choice cards, updatedPermissions for "always allow"), includePartialMessages for live streaming, PermissionRequest hook to fire push notifications, and the shared ~/.claude/projects store so sessions started on the phone are resumable in the laptop CLI with `claude --resume <id>` and vice versa. Tier 2 (other agents, ACP): embed an ACP client using @agentclientprotocol/sdk and spawn Gemini CLI (`--experimental-acp`) and Codex (via @agentclientprotocol/codex-acp) as ACP subprocesses — session/request_permission and session/update map almost 1:1 onto the same approvals-inbox and streaming model, so one ACP client covers every future ACP agent for free. Tier 3 (everything else + plain terminals): node-pty wrapping with raw output streaming and keystroke injection, no structured approvals. Normalize all three tiers into one event schema modeled on ACP's shapes (tool-call status lifecycle + four permission option kinds), since that is the intersection all backends can express.
pitfalls: canUseTool never fires for auto-approved tools — anything matched by an allow rule or acceptEdits/bypassPermissions bypasses the phone inbox silently; use a PreToolUse hook if you also want an activity feed of auto-approved actions.
Claude session resume is keyed to the encoded cwd: resuming from a different working directory silently creates a fresh empty session instead of erroring. The hub daemon must pin cwd per session.

Do not let the laptop CLI and the hub daemon drive the same Claude session ID at the same time — sessions are effectively single-writer JSONL files; treat attach as exclusive (concurrent behavior unverified).

ACP capabilities are optional per agent: feature-detect loadSession/sessionCapabilities.resume at initialize. Cold-restart session recovery through ACP is unreliable today — keep your own transcript mirror in the hub rather than relying on session/load replay.
If you shell out to `codex exec` you get zero approval prompts (sandbox-only safety) — Codex approvals require app-server mode or the codex-acp adapter. Choose ACP/app-server for Codex, not exec.
The zed-industries adapter repos were archived and moved to the @agentclientprotocol npm org (claude-agent-acp, codex-acp) — depend on the new package names or you stop getting updates.
In ACP, terminals are a CLIENT capability: your hub must implement the terminal methods if you want ACP agents' shell commands streamed live; the agent won't provide them.
includePartialMessages is a firehose of raw API stream deltas — batch/throttle before relaying over the phone link, and don't persist every delta.

PTY-wrapping gives no structured events: approval detection means scraping TUI output, which breaks on every agent UI redesign. Happy already solved this at scale (MIT) — study or reuse before rebuilding.
An approval pending in canUseTool keeps the Node process pinned; if the daemon must restart, use the defer hook decision and resume the session rather than losing the pending prompt.

TS SDK: don't build on the removed V2 createSession API (gone in 0.3.142); Python's canUseTool needs streaming-input mode plus a dummy-hook workaround — another reason to keep the daemon in TypeScript.

domain: Phone-side client: standalone app stack, push notification pipeline, actionable approvals, background/reconnect model, terminal rendering, and personal-device distribution (July 2026)
recommendation: Build the phone client as an Expo (React Native + TypeScript) app with expo-dev-client — not a PWA: on iOS, web push has no action buttons and materially worse delivery, which kills the core "approve from the lock screen" requirement. Pay the $99/yr Apple Developer Program (non-negotiable for APNs) and distribute via TestFlight internal testing (easiest updates; re-upload every 90 days) or EAS internal-distribution ad-hoc builds (1-year profile, no Apple processing); for Android, EAS-build an APK and sideload, registering the free 20-device limited-distribution account when verification enforcement reaches you. Notification pipeline: laptop daemon -> HTTPS POST to Expo Push Service -> APNs/FCM; register an "approval" notification category with Approve and Deny actions (Deny with a text-input action for a steering reply), set interruption-level=time-sensitive, and treat every push as a signal carrying only IDs — the app fetches authoritative state from the daemon on open. Handle action taps with opensAppToForeground:false plus an idempotent, approval-ID-scoped API call, and make tapping the notification body deep-link to the approvals inbox as the guaranteed fallback. Architect all live features as reconnect-and-catch-up: one WebSocket while foregrounded, torn down on background, with every event stream cursor-addressed on the daemon so the app replays from its last-seen sequence number on resume — never assume the socket survived. Render agent/log output as a FlashList of plain-text lines (cheap, selectable, searchable), and reserve a real xterm.js-in-WebView view (pattern: @fressh/react-native-xtermjs-webview, with write coalescing and a custom key toolbar for Ctrl/Esc/arrows) only for interactive terminal sessions.
pitfalls: Trying to stay free-tier on iOS: a free Personal Team has no push entitlement and builds die every 7 days — the app becomes a weekly chore and can never notify. Budget the $99/yr from day one.

Expo Go cannot receive remote push notifications (support removed around SDK 53) — you must use a development build / dev-client from the start, so set up EAS or local builds before writing notification code. [Expo docs FAQ; verify exact SDK cutoff]

Designing as if the phone holds a connection: iOS suspends the app seconds after backgrounding and background URLSession does not support WebSockets. If the daemon treats socket-drop as 'user gone', approvals will hang. Every stream needs server-side buffering + cursor replay.
Silent/content-available background pushes on iOS are throttled and best-effort — do not use them for state sync; sync on foreground + visible pushes only.

Notification action taps with the app killed are the least reliable path on both platforms (Android had years of no-op bugs; iOS background JS handling in Expo has edge cases). Make Approve/Deny idempotent with server-side expiry, show a confirmation push/badge after the action lands, and always keep tap-to-open-inbox as the fallback. Test killed-state actions on real devices in week one.

Expo push tickets and receipts do not mean the notification reached the device — the approval must also be visible in the in-app inbox, and the daemon should re-notify (escalating) if an approval sits unanswered. Also handle DeviceNotRegistered receipts by rotating stored tokens.
APNs payloads are capped at 4 KB — never embed diffs/tool output in the push; send IDs and fetch over your API.

xterm.js in a WebView is fine for output but mobile keyboards are the hard part: no Ctrl/Esc/Tab/arrow keys natively, autocorrect interferes. Budget for a custom accessory key row; and coalesce writes across the RN<->WebView bridge or fast output (builds, agent streams) will freeze the UI.

Do not render agent streaming output through xterm.js by default — a virtualized text list (FlashList) is far cheaper, supports copy/search, and matches chat-style UX; keep the terminal emulator only for real PTY sessions.
TestFlight internal builds expire after 90 days — set a calendar reminder or CI cron to re-upload, or the app stops launching mid-trip.

Android-side surprise: from Sept 2026 (region-staged, global 2027) sideloaded APKs on certified devices need developer verification; the free 20-device limited-distribution account covers personal use but is a new signup step mid-project.
Time Sensitive notifications require declaring the capability and can be disabled per-app by the user in Settings — degrade gracefully to normal priority rather than assuming breakthrough delivery.

domain: Secure phone-to-laptop connectivity for remote agent control (Tailscale vs Cloudflare Tunnel vs self-hosted E2E relay), push path, and daemon threat model
recommendation: Use Tailscale-direct as the transport: install Tailscale on the laptop and iPhone (2 devices, 1 user — comfortably inside the free Personal plan), run the daemon as a Node/TS process that binds only to the laptop's Tailscale 100.x address (never 0.0.0.0), and serve HTTPS+WSS under the laptop's ts.net MagicDNS name using `tailscale serve` or a Caddy-managed cert so the Expo app gets real TLS with no ATS exceptions. The Expo app dials `laptop.<tailnet>.ts.net` through the system-wide Tailscale tunnel with VPN On Demand's *.ts.net hostname trigger, so the user never manually toggles the VPN; no Tailscale SDK embedding is required. On top of the WireGuard layer, add app-level auth: QR-code pairing on the laptop that hands the phone a per-device random token (stored hashed on the laptop, revocable, shown in a device list), and design the daemon API as typed operations only — approve/deny(promptId), sendText(sessionId), startSession(dir ∈ allowlisted project roots), attachTerminal(id) — never a generic exec endpoint, with an append-only audit log of every mutating call. Push notifications go laptop → Expo push API → APNs with content-free payloads ("A session needs your attention"); the phone fetches details over the tunnel, so nothing sensitive ever transits Expo/Apple. This gives zero public endpoints, zero relays to operate, and E2E encryption by default (WireGuard device-to-device). If the tool were ever shared with other people, do not invite them into the tailnet; switch the transport to the Happy model (self-hosted WSS relay with per-user NaCl keys and client-side encryption of everything, including stored credentials — learn from Happy #680) or Cloudflare Access with per-user SSO, because once a third-party relay or Cloudflare's edge sits in the path, payload-level E2E and per-user identity become mandatory rather than optional.
pitfalls: Apple tax is unavoidable for the 'standalone app + push' requirement: free Apple accounts have no push entitlement and free-provisioned builds die after 7 days. Budget $99/yr and distribute via TestFlight. (Android/Expo push has no equivalent cost.)
Tailscale's 180-day node key expiry will silently take the laptop offline while you're away — disable key expiry on the laptop node (or tag it) on day one.

The *.ts.net on-demand trigger only fires when the interface rule is 'Do Nothing' and only when the app dials the MagicDNS hostname (not a raw 100.x IP); the first request after the tunnel was down can time out while WireGuard establishes — build connect-retry into the app.
React Native fetch/WebSocket to plain http://100.x.y.z hits iOS App Transport Security; use the ts.net Let's Encrypt cert instead of sprinkling ATS exceptions.
`tailscale cert` files are NOT auto-renewed (90-day expiry) — use `tailscale serve` or Caddy so renewal is automatic, or the app breaks mid-trip in month 4.

Never put notification content in Expo pushes: payloads transit Expo and APNs in plaintext. Also treat the ExponentPushToken as a secret (anyone holding it can spam the phone) and enable Expo's push-security access tokens.

Cloudflare path looks 'free and easy' but the edge reads your plaintext command channel, and a service token baked into a phone app is a static long-lived bearer credential — worse than the Tailscale design on both counts for remote command execution.

Self-hosted relay path: E2E only covers what you actually encrypt client-side — Happy shipped 'E2E encrypted' marketing while storing API keys decryptable by the server (Discussion #680). You also inherit an internet-facing service to patch, plus metadata leakage (IPs, timing, message sizes).

Threat-model mitigations that are actually required: stolen phone → keys/token in iOS Keychain via expo-secure-store behind Face ID, plus two revocation paths (delete device token on daemon; remove phone from tailnet admin console); leaked token → per-device tokens stored hashed, revocable individually, audit log to spot misuse; LAN attacker → daemon bound to tailnet interface only, so home Wi-Fi devices can't even reach the port; relay compromise → N/A in Tailscale-direct (no relay).

A command allowlist matters less than API shape: expose typed operations (approve promptId, send text, start agent in allowlisted dirs) rather than a generic shell-exec endpoint — the terminal-control feature is inherently arbitrary execution, so gate terminal attach behind a separate per-session confirmation and log all input.
The laptop will sleep and kill everything: set pmset / caffeinate / 'prevent sleep when plugged in', or the phone app's first real-world failure will be 'laptop unreachable'.
Battery on iPhone: fine as long as the laptop is never used as an exit node; the documented worst case is exit-node routing, which this design doesn't need.

domain: Prior art: phone control of AI coding agents and terminals (July 2026)
recommendation: Do not build the relay server, E2E encryption, mobile app, or session-spawning daemon from scratch — Happy (MIT, 22.9k stars, active) already implements roughly 90% of the brief: sessions list, approvals with push notifications, steering, live streaming, remote spawn via daemon, multi-agent (Claude/Codex/ACP), iOS+Android+web, and a self-hostable single-container server. Verdict per option: ADOPT Happy as the core (self-host the server if the public relay flakes); ADOPT Claude Code's built-in Remote Control as the zero-maintenance baseline for Claude-only sessions plus Dispatch for remote kickoff; BORROW Paseo's daemon-orchestrator architecture only if Copilot/OpenCode support matters (AGPL discourages forking); IGNORE Omnara (OSS version deprecated, product now closed); keep Tailscale + Blink/mosh/tmux or VibeTunnel as the plain-terminal fallback layer rather than writing a terminal transport. The single genuine gap versus the brief is unified plain-terminal control inside the same phone app — if that is non-negotiable, FORK Happy (MIT) and add a terminal session type to the happy-cli daemon and Expo app, an additive feature on a maintained codebase instead of months of greenfield infra. Omnara's deprecation is the cautionary tale: never hand-roll a Claude Code TUI wrapper; anything custom should sit on the Claude Agent SDK, which is exactly the migration Omnara made.
pitfalls: Wrapping the Claude Code CLI/TUI is a maintenance treadmill — Omnara publicly deprecated their wrapper for this exact reason; build on the Agent SDK or adopt a maintained wrapper (Happy) instead.
A 'standalone phone app' means Apple Developer account, App Store review, and APNs push-certificate upkeep forever — Happy and Paseo already carry that burden; a home-grown app pays it for one user.
iOS backgrounding kills long-lived sockets; real push (APNs/FCM) requires server infrastructure — another reason a self-built solution quietly grows a relay service.

Claude Code Remote Control eligibility is fragile: DISABLE_TELEMETRY, DO_NOT_TRACK, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC, or a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL silently disable it, and API-key auth never works.

Remote Control stores session transcripts on Anthropic servers (not E2E encrypted) and each server is bound to its launch directory — 'pick any project dir from the phone' needs one server per project or a daemon like Happy's.
Happy's hosted relay (api.cluster-fluster.com) has had outages/timeouts; plan to self-host (standalone Docker image, HAPPY_SERVER_URL) from day one if reliability matters.
Exposing a terminal via ttyd/VibeTunnel is remote code execution — keep it inside Tailscale, never on a public tunnel with basic auth alone.
Paseo is AGPL-3.0: fine for personal use, contaminating if the user ever wants to open-source a derived product under a permissive license (Happy's MIT is safer to fork).

The VS Code Claude extension chat panel is not scriptable by other extensions, and vscode.dev on a phone is desktop UI — do not plan an IDE-side integration path; /remote-control from the extension is the supported hook.
Raw Claude Code TUI over SSH on a phone flickers and has painful copy/paste (reported by Happy self-hoster) — mosh+tmux is a fallback, not the daily driver for agent sessions.
